claim: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a global public health concern due to the rising myriad of hypervirulent and multidrug-resistant clones associated with high mortality.
source: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a global public health concern due to the rising myriad of hypervirulent and multidrug-resistant clones both alarmingly associated with high mortality.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references the clinical significance of K. pneumoniae, drawing on established knowledge about this pathogen.

claim: A total of 427 genes were identified as essential for growth on LB agar in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Through transposon directed insertion-site sequencing (TraDIS), a total of 427 genes were identified as essential for growth on LB agar, whereas transposon insertions in 11 and 144 genes decreased fitness for growth in either urine or serum, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the TraDIS experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transposon insertions in 11 genes decreased fitness for growth in urine.
source: Through transposon directed insertion-site sequencing (TraDIS), a total of 427 genes were identified as essential for growth on LB agar, whereas transposon insertions in 11 and 144 genes decreased fitness for growth in either urine or serum, respectively.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental TraDIS data from urine growth experiments.

claim: Transposon insertions in 144 genes decreased fitness for growth in serum.
source: Through transposon directed insertion-site sequencing (TraDIS), a total of 427 genes were identified as essential for growth on LB agar, whereas transposon insertions in 11 and 144 genes decreased fitness for growth in either urine or serum, respectively.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental TraDIS data from serum growth experiments.

claim: K. pneumoniae can colonize multiple body sites causing infections ranging from pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and bacteremia in immunocompromised patients and those with comorbidities.
source: In immunocompromised patients, and those with comorbidities such as diabetes or alcoholism, K. pneumoniae can colonize multiple body sites causing a diverse array of infections ranging from life-threatening pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and bacteremia (Ko et al., 2002; Gonçalves Barbosa et al., 2022; Tumbarello et al., 2015; Clegg and Murphy, 2016; Paczosa and Mecsas, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: K. pneumoniae is a frequently reported multidrug-resistant pathogen isolated from nosocomial settings.
source: K. pneumoniae is a frequently reported multidrug-resistant pathogen isolated from nosocomial settings.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about K. pneumoniae epidemiology.

claim: Nosocomial K. pneumoniae infections have higher mortality rates and require longer treatment regimens and hospital stays.
source: Such infections have generally higher mortality rates and require longer treatment regimens and hospital stays, placing a significant burden on healthcare providers (GBD 2019 Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022; Pham et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Resistance to β-lactam antibiotics in K. pneumoniae is mediated by horizontally acquired plasmid-mediated β-lactamases.
source: Of most concern is resistance to β-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin, aztreonam, and extended-spectrum cephalosporins, by horizontally acquired plasmid-mediated β-lactamases (Navon-Venezia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Pandrug-resistant K. pneumoniae strains have emerged.
source: While combined antibiotic therapies have been deployed in the clinic, the emergence of pandrug-resistant strains has created an urgency to develop new and efficient approaches to treat K. pneumoniae infections (Garbati and Al Godhair, 2013; Campos et al., 2016; Rojas et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Distinct lineages of K. pneumoniae exist in clinical and environmental settings.
source: Recent large-scale phylogenetic investigations have suggested that distinct lineages of K. pneumoniae exist in clinical and environmental settings (Wyres et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Two clinical pathotypes of K. pneumoniae have emerged: classical and hypervirulent.
source: Furthermore, two clinical pathotypes of K. pneumoniae have emerged: classical and hypervirulent.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about K. pneumoniae classification.

claim: Genes involved in adhesion, iron acquisition, capsulation, and cell envelope biogenesis are important for K. pneumoniae virulence.
source: While the full repertoire of genetic factors required for K. pneumoniae virulence remains unclear, various studies have highlighted the importance of genes involved in adhesion, iron acquisition, capsulation, and cell envelope biogenesis (Marques et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The ability to colonize the urinary tract and survive in the bloodstream are essential pathogenic traits for both classical and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae strains.
source: Nevertheless, for both classical and hypervirulent K. pneumoniae strains, the ability to colonize the urinary tract and survive in the bloodstream are essential pathogenic traits and are dependent on a large and diverse range of virulence factors (Bengoechea and Sa Pessoa, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: LPS O-antigens and capsular polysaccharide K-antigens contribute to resistance of serum-mediated killing and antiphagocytosis in K. pneumoniae.
source: Indeed, previous studies demonstrated that lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (O-) (9 serotypes) and capsular polysaccharide (cps) (K-) antigens (79 serotypes) contribute to the resistance of serum-mediated killing and antiphagocytosis (Choi et al., 2020; Martin and Bachman, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Serum resistance in Gram-negative bacteria is defined by a multitude of factors (the serum resistome).
source: However, prior genetic screens have revealed that serum resistance in Gram-negative bacteria is an intricate phenotype defined by a multitude of factors (the serum resistome) (Short et al., 2020; Phan et al., 2013; McCarthy and Taylor, 2022; Ondari et al., 2019; Subashchandrabose et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A recent study identified 93 different genes associated with serum resistance across four distinct K. pneumoniae strains, with only three genes (lpp, arnD, and rfaH) playing a role in all strains.
source: A recent study of K. pneumoniae identified 93 different genes associated with serum resistance across four distinct strains but found that only three genes (lpp, arnD, and rfaH) played a role in all strains.
evidence: This claim references findings from a previous study, implicitly citing published literature.

claim: Multiple mechanisms of serum resistance may exist in Klebsiella lineages.
source: These data hint that multiple mechanisms of serum resistance may exist in Klebsiella lineages.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that different genes are required for serum resistance in different strains.

claim: The full repertoire of genes required for growth of K. pneumoniae in the urinary tract (the urinome) has not been defined.
source: In contrast, the full repertoire of genes required for growth of K. pneumoniae in the urinary tract (the urinome) has not been defined.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: K. pneumoniae ECL8 is a member of the K2-ST375 phylogenetic lineage.
source: In this study, we generated a highly saturated transposon library within K. pneumoniae ECL8, a member of the K2-ST375 phylogenetic lineage that includes hypervirulent clones of epidemiological significance known to cause infections in relatively healthy subjects predominantly in Asia (Hoashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the strain used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: K2-ST375 includes hypervirulent clones known to cause infections in relatively healthy subjects predominantly in Asia.
source: In this study, we generated a highly saturated transposon library within K. pneumoniae ECL8, a member of the K2-ST375 phylogenetic lineage that includes hypervirulent clones of epidemiological significance known to cause infections in relatively healthy subjects predominantly in Asia (Hoashi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A K. pneumoniae ECL8 mini-Tn5 mutant library composed of >1 million mutants was constructed.
source: A K. pneumoniae ECL8 mini-Tn5 mutant library composed of >1 million mutants was constructed and subsequently subjected to TraDIS.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The K. pneumoniae ECL8 reference genome consists of an ~5.3 Mb chromosome and a single 205 kb plasmid.
source: The resulting reads were mapped to the reference genome that consists of an ~5.3 Mb chromosome and a single 205 kb plasmid (EMBL Accessions: HF536482.1 and HF536483) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the reference genome data and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The gene insertion index scores (IIS) of the two technical replicates of the K. pneumoniae ECL8 TraDIS library (KTL1 and KTL2) were highly correlated with each other (R2=0.955).
source: The gene insertion index scores (IIS) of the two technical replicates of the K. pneumoniae ECL8 TraDIS library (KTL1 and KTL2) were highly correlated with each other (R2=0.955), demonstrating a high level of reproducibility (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The K. pneumoniae ECL8 TraDIS library contained 554,834 unique genome-wide transposon insertion sites.
source: This library contained 554,834 unique genome-wide transposon insertion sites and 499,919 of these insertions map within annotated coding sequence (CDS) boundaries.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: 499,919 transposon insertions map within annotated coding sequence (CDS) boundaries in the K. pneumoniae ECL8 library.
source: This library contained 554,834 unique genome-wide transposon insertion sites and 499,919 of these insertions map within annotated coding sequence (CDS) boundaries.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claim: The K. pneumoniae ECL8 TraDIS library has an average transposon insertion every 9.93 bp throughout the genome.
source: This high level of transposon coverage equates to an average transposon insertion every 9.93 bp throughout the genome, equivalent to an insertion approximately every four codons.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data.

claim: The K. pneumoniae ECL8 plasmid is likely present as a single copy.
source: A de Brujin graph visualized in the genome assembly package Bandage revealed that the sequencing coverage of the plasmid was only 1.33-fold higher than that of the chromosome indicating that the plasmid is likely present as a single copy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Wick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing coverage data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 373 chromosomal genes were classified as essential for growth on solid LB medium supplemented with kanamycin in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Based on the above criteria, 373 chromosomal genes were assigned a log2-LR of less than –3.6 and were therefore classified as essential for growth on solid Luria-Bertani (LB) medium supplemented with kanamycin (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the bimodal analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: Most genes (4551) in K. pneumoniae ECL8 were classified as non-essential.
source: Most genes (4551) were classified as non-essential (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is directly supported by the bimodal analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: A subset of 241 genes in K. pneumoniae ECL8 had their essentiality mode deemed 'unclear'.
source: A subset of 241 genes were located between these two modes with their essentiality mode being deemed 'unclear' (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is directly supported by the bimodal analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: No essential genes were identified within the COG categories for chromatin structure and dynamics (B), cell motility (N), and secondary structure (Q) in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: We identified no essential genes within the COG categories for chromatin structure and dynamics (B), cell motility (N), and secondary structure (Q) suggesting genes within these categories are not required or redundant for K. pneumoniae growth in the utilized nutrient-rich liquid medium.
evidence: This is based on the COG enrichment analysis of essential genes.

claim: Genes involved in translation (J), cell cycle control (D), and co-enzyme metabolism (H) were the most highly enriched among essential genes in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: However, genes involved in signal transduction (T) and inorganic ion transport/metabolism (P) were depleted, while genes involved in translation (J), cell cycle control (D), and co-enzyme metabolism (H) were the most highly enriched.
evidence: This is based on the COG enrichment analysis of essential genes shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The enriched COG categories among essential genes in K. pneumoniae ECL8 correlate with those in other Proteobacteria such as Salmonella enterica Typhimurium, S. enterica Typhi, and Caulobacter crescentus.
source: This correlates with enriched COG categories shared among essential genes in other members of the Proteobacteria such as Salmonella enterica Typhimurium, S. enterica Typhi, and Caulobacter crescentus and serves as an internal control for the validity of the library (Christen et al., 2011; Grazziotin et al., 2015; Barquist et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature and serves as validation of the experimental approach.

claim: 11 genes on the K. pneumoniae ECL8 plasmid met the criteria to be defined as essential.
source: The identification of 11 genes on the K. pneumoniae ECL8 plasmid that met the criteria to be defined as essential was an unexpected observation (Table 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the results and shown in Table 2.

claim: The bacterial copy number of the K. pneumoniae ECL8 plasmid was approximated to be one.
source: As previously noted, the bacterial copy number of the plasmid was approximated to be one.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing coverage data.

claim: The 11 plasmid-borne 'essential' genes in K. pneumoniae ECL8 are likely required for plasmid replication and stability and are unlikely to be essential for growth.
source: Notably, the 11 plasmid-borne 'essential' genes included repB, which is required for plasmid replication. Therefore, these genes are likely to be required for plasmid replication and stability and are unlikely to be essential for growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the function of repB and previous observations about plasmid curing.

claim: K. pneumoniae remains viable when large indigenous virulence plasmids are cured from the bacterium.
source: This hypothesis is supported by previous observations that K. pneumoniae remains viable when large indigenous virulence plasmids are cured from the bacterium (Tang et al., 2010; Rodríguez-Medina et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A total of 667 genomic regions with insertion-free regions (IFRs) ≥145 bp were identified in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: A total of 667 genomic regions with IFRs≥145 bp were identified, many which correspond to the 380 essential genes identified through the bimodal analysis described earlier.
evidence: This is directly stated based on the IFR analysis.

claim: 54 additional genes with statistically significant IFRs were identified in K. pneumoniae ECL8, indicating they are likely essential for growth.
source: Aside from those genes already identified by the bimodal analyses described above, our analyses revealed 54 additional genes with statistically significant IFRs, which indicates that they are likely essential for growth under the conditions tested here.
evidence: This is based on the IFR analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: K. pneumoniae ECL8 contains at least 427 essential genes.
source: Thus, our data suggest K. pneumoniae contains at least 427 essential genes, which we define as the ECL8 curated essential gene list.
evidence: This is the sum of genes identified as essential through bimodal analysis and IFR analysis.

claim: 59 regions ≥145 bp that lacked transposon insertion sites did not map to within annotated CDS boundaries in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Interestingly, the methodology used here revealed 59 regions ≥145 bp that lacked transposon insertion sites and did not map to within annotated CDS boundaries (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on the IFR analysis of the TraDIS data.

claim: 46 of the 59 unannotated IFRs in K. pneumoniae ECL8 contain potential ORFs that could encode proteins through blastX identification.
source: Forty-six of these regions contain potential ORFs that could encode proteins through blastX identification.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis of the unannotated IFRs.

claim: Directional insertion bias of the Tn5 transposon was noted within the cps operon encoding the K2 capsule in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Directional insertion bias of the transposon was noted within a large genomic region of ~14 kb encoding the virulence-associated cps operon (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the TraDIS data and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The K. pneumoniae ECL8 cps operon encodes a KL2/K2 capsule with 18/18 of the expected genes.
source: The bioinformatic webtool 'Kaptive' determined with high confidence the K. pneumoniae ECL8 cps operon encodes for a KL2/K2 capsule with 18/18 of the expected genes (Figure 7—source data 1; Lam et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis using the Kaptive tool.

claim: Transposon insertions in the forward orientation were poorly tolerated in the K. pneumoniae ECL8 cps operon.
source: Notably, transposon insertions were poorly tolerated in the forward Tn orientation of the DNA strand.
evidence: This is directly observed in the TraDIS data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: This study is the first to describe transposon insertion bias across an entire operon.
source: While bias for Tn insertions has previously been described in individual genes (e.g. ribosomal RNA genes), this study is the first to describe such a large bias across an operon (Goodall et al., 2018; Christen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the observation, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: 57% of the essential genes identified in K. pneumoniae ECL8 were essential in three other K. pneumoniae strains (KPNIH1, RH201207, and ATCC 43816).
source: While further validation experiments will be required to determine whether specific genes are essential, 57% of the essential genes identified in K. pneumoniae ECL8 were essential in the other three strains.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of essential gene lists from different studies.

claim: The K. pneumoniae ECL8 transposon library is among the most saturated K. pneumoniae libraries reported to date.
source: Furthermore, our transposon mutant library is among the most saturated K. pneumoniae libraries reported to date, permitting accurate determination of gene essentiality and delineating between real and stochastic effects.
evidence: This is based on comparison of transposon insertion density with other published libraries.

claim: Ten genes that satisfied a stringent threshold (log2FC>–2 and Q-value≤0.05) were considered advantageous for K. pneumoniae ECL8 growth in urine.
source: Ten genes that satisfied a stringent threshold of a log2 fold change (log2FC)>–2 and a Q-value≤0.05, relative to the LB control, were considered as advantageous for K. pneumoniae ECL8 growth in urine (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the TraDIS analysis of growth in urine.

claim: Genes encoding SodA, OmpA, Skp, and proteins associated with iron acquisition (fepB, fepD, fepG, exbB, and exbD) were essential for K. pneumoniae ECL8 growth in urine.
source: These included genes encoding the superoxide dismutase SodA, the structural outer membrane protein OmpA (Pain et al., 2015), the periplasmic chaperone Skp (Mas et al., 2019), and five proteins (fepB, fepD, fepG, exbB, and exbD) associated with iron acquisition (Caza and Kronstad, 2013).
evidence: This is directly supported by the TraDIS analysis of growth in urine.

claim: ytfL and argH play key roles in controlling cytoplasmic cadaverine and putrescine concentrations and amino acid biosynthesis, respectively.
source: The remaining two genes (ytfL and argH) play key roles in controlling cytoplasmic cadaverine and putrescine concentrations and amino acid biosynthesis, respectively (Iwadate et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A ΔsodA::aph mutant was less fit than wild-type K. pneumoniae ECL8 in both urine and LB, but the phenotype was exacerbated in urine.
source: When compared to the WT, a ΔsodA::aph mutant was less fit in both urine and LB, but the phenotype was exacerbated in urine.
evidence: This is directly supported by the competitive index experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The fitness of ompA, fepB, fepD, exbB, and exbD mutants was comparable to the parent strain when grown in LB medium and only less fit when grown in urine.
source: In contrast, the fitness of the remaining mutants was comparable to the parent strain when grown in LB medium and only less fit when grown in urine.
evidence: This is directly supported by the competitive index experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Iron levels are limiting growth in human urine and the ability to acquire iron is crucial for K. pneumoniae to survive and grow in vivo.
source: Based on these observations, we hypothesized that iron levels were limiting growth in human urine and that the ability to acquire iron was crucial for K. pneumoniae to survive and grow in vivo (Cassat and Skaar, 2013; Banerjee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: Supplementation of urine with exogenous ferrous iron (100 μM FeSO4) increased K. pneumoniae ECL8 growth relative to non-supplemented cultures.
source: In contrast, supplementation of urine with exogenous iron increased growth relative to non-supplemented cultures with no difference in growth upon passage (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly supported by the growth experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Addition of the iron chelator 2,2-dipyridyl to urine further exacerbated the restricted growth of K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: However, the optical density of K. pneumoniae cultures decreased after passage in urine (Figure 5B), and the restricted growth was further exacerbated by the addition of the iron chelator 2,2-dipyridyl (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the growth experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mutants lacking genes involved in iron uptake (fepB, fepD, exbB, exbD) were drastically less fit than wild-type K. pneumoniae ECL8 in urine.
source: Not unexpectedly, area under the curve analysis revealed that mutants lacking genes involved in iron uptake (fepB, fepD, exbB, exbD) were drastically less fit than the WT (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is directly supported by the growth kinetics experiments shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Loss of the Ferric Uptake Regulator (fur) gene is beneficial for K. pneumoniae ECL8 growth in urine.
source: In contrast, the highest log2FC increase (~7-fold) in read counts mapped to the Ferric Uptake Regulator (fur) gene indicating its loss is beneficial for growth in urine.
evidence: This is directly supported by the TraDIS analysis of growth in urine.

claim: The Fur regulon plays a pivotal role for K. pneumoniae growth in urine by tightly regulating enterobactin synthesis and enterobactin-mediated iron uptake.
source: Altogether, this suggests that the Fur regulon plays a pivotal role for K. pneumoniae growth in urine by tightly regulating enterobactin synthesis and enterobactin-mediated iron uptake.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TraDIS data and known functions of Fur.

claim: A 2 log10 decrease in the number of viable K. pneumoniae ECL8 cells was observed after 90 min exposure to normal human serum.
source: In contrast, a 2 log10 decrease in the number of viable K. pneumoniae cells was observed after 90 min exposure to normal human serum, and a >4 log10 decrease after 180 min exposure.
evidence: This is directly supported by the serum killing kinetics experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: No reduction in viable K. pneumoniae ECL8 cells was noted when incubated in heat-inactivated serum.
source: To determine whether the observed reduction in viable cells was due to the presence of active complement proteins, K. pneumoniae was incubated in heat-inactivated serum control where no reduction in viable was noted (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by the serum killing kinetics experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A total of 356 genes with a log2FC≤–2, p<0.05, and Q-value of ≤0.05 between serum and heat-inactivated control were classified as advantageous for growth under complement-mediated killing conditions.
source: A total of 356 genes with a log2FC≤–2, p<0.05, and Q-value of ≤0.05 between the serum and heat-inactivated control were classified as genes that are advantageous for growth under complement-mediated killing conditions (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the TraDIS analysis of growth in serum.

claim: Operons encoding LPS core antigen, O-antigen, and enterobacterial common antigen biosynthesis contain several conditionally essential genes for serum resistance in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: The operons encoding LPS core antigen, O-antigen, and enterobacterial common antigen biosynthesis were noted as containing several conditionally essential genes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the TraDIS analysis of growth in serum shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutants defective in LPS core antigen, O-antigen, and enterobacterial common antigen biosynthesis have been reported to play a role in membrane integrity and resistance to serum killing for a variety of Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Mutants defective in these cell envelope structures have previously been reported to play a role in membrane integrity and resistance to serum killing for a variety of Gram-negative bacteria (Onsare et al., 2015; Salamon et al., 2020; Rai and Mitchell, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ΔwbbY::aph mutant was more sensitive to human serum than the parent K. pneumoniae ECL8 strain with no viable mutants surviving after 30 min.
source: However, the ΔwbbY::aph mutant was more sensitive to human serum than the parent with no viable mutants surviving after 30 min (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is directly supported by the serum bactericidal assay shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The ΔwbbY::aph strain produced LPS with a lower molecular weight compared to the parent K. pneumoniae ECL8 strain, suggesting that a truncated O-antigen was expressed.
source: The ΔwbbY::aph strain produced LPS with a lower molecular weight compared to the parent strain, suggesting that a truncated O-antigen was expressed.
evidence: This is directly supported by the LPS profile analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Deletion of wbbY in K. pneumoniae NTUH-K2044 (ST23) resulted in LPS profile defects due to abrogated D-galactan II production.
source: Importantly, Hsieh et al. have previously reported that deletion by wbbY in K. pneumoniae NTUH-K2044 (ST23) resulted in LPS profile defects due to abrogated D-galactan II production (Hsieh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Genes with the greatest significance in decreased insertions following serum exposure for 180 min were O-antigen outer-core biosynthesis gene espJ_2/wabI and O-antigen ligase rfaL/waaL.
source: As expected, similar to our previous experiment genes with the greatest significance in decreased insertions, suggesting decreased fitness, were O-antigen outer-core biosynthesis gene espJ_2/wabI and O-antigen ligase rfaL/waaL (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly supported by the AlbaTraDIS analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Genes with significantly increased insertions following serum exposure for 180 min included hns, gnd, and igaA.
source: Genes with significantly increased insertions, suggesting increased fitness, included hns, gnd, and igaA (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is directly supported by the AlbaTraDIS analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The hns::aph mutant was more resistant to serum than wild-type K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: To determine whether the hns mutant was indeed more resistant to serum a sample of 1×108 cells was incubated in serum for 360 min. At 30 min post-incubation the number of viable hns::aph cells was decreased by ~2 log. However, no additional decrease in viable cell numbers was observed at later time points and these strains proliferated in serum (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is directly supported by the serum killing assay shown in Figure 7F.

claim: rcsA, galF, wzi, and manC were derepressed in a Δhns K. pneumoniae mutant resulting in increased capsule production.
source: Ares and colleagues demonstrated that rcsA; galF; wzi; and manC were derepressed in a Δhns K. pneumoniae mutant resulting in increased capsule production (Ares et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Activation of the Rcs regulon confers resistance to serum killing in K. pneumoniae by increasing capsule production.
source: These data suggest that activation of the Rcs regulon confers resistance to serum killing in K. pneumoniae, as noted for other members of the Enterobacteriaceae, by increasing capsule production (Meng et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: Sequence reads mapping to gnd were enriched for the forward orientation of the transposon only.
source: Interestingly, sequence reads mapping to gnd were enriched for the forward orientation of the transposon only (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the TraDIS data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Transposon insertions in the forward orientation in gnd have transcriptional read-through driving expression of the downstream neighboring gene manC and more distal O-antigen biosynthesis genes.
source: Transposon insertions in this orientation have transcriptional read-through driving expression of the downstream neighboring gene manC and more distal O-antigen biosynthesis genes (i.e. rfb cluster) (Follador et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the transposon insertion orientation and supported by a citation.

claim: The manC gene encodes mannose-1-phosphate guanylyltransferase that is required for the synthesis of capsule.
source: The manC gene encodes mannose-1-phosphate guanylyltransferase that is required for the synthesis of capsule, and as noted above, upregulation of manC results in increased production of capsule.
evidence: This is a statement about the known function of manC.

claim: Upregulation of manC results in increased production of capsule in K. pneumoniae.
source: The manC gene encodes mannose-1-phosphate guanylyltransferase that is required for the synthesis of capsule, and as noted above, upregulation of manC results in increased production of capsule.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations about hns and gnd mutants.

claim: The high density of insertion sites achieved in this study ensured reliable identification of essential and conditionally essential genes and a low probability of false-positive identification.
source: Nevertheless, the high density of insertion sites achieved in our study ensured reliable identification of essential and conditionally essential genes and a low probability of false-positive identification, which had previously been noted for low complexity libraries (Chao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of the library and is supported by a citation.

claim: The study revealed only 11 genes significantly required for growth in urine.
source: Unexpectedly, our study revealed only 11 genes significantly required for growth in urine.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The non-essential nature of fepA and fepC for growth in urine might be the result of functional redundancy due to paralogous copies.
source: First, as K. pneumoniae ECL8 contains paralogous copies of fepA (fepA_1 and fepA_2) and fepC (fepC_1 and fepC_2), the non-essential nature of fepA and fepC might be the result of functional redundancy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genomic content of K. pneumoniae ECL8.

claim: Mutants lacking enterobactin (or aerobactin) synthesis and export genes can 'cheat' by acquiring the siderophore released from siderophore-producing strains within the population.
source: Second, as TraDIS is in principle a large-scale competition experiment between thousands of mutants, mutants lacking enterobactin (or aerobactin) synthesis and export genes can 'cheat' by acquiring the siderophore released from siderophore-producing strains within the population, a phenomenon described previously (Butaitė et al., 2017; Holden and Bachman, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of TraDIS experiments and supported by citations.

claim: The serum resistome of K. pneumoniae ECL8 consisted of more than 144 genes.
source: In contrast to the limited number of genes in the urinome, the serum resistome consisted of more than 144 genes.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: A recent study found 93 genes that were required for survival in one or more K. pneumoniae strains, with only three genes (rfaH, lpp, and arnD) common to all four strains.
source: This number is significantly greater than reports of a recent study that defined the serum resistome of four independent K. pneumoniae strains (Short et al., 2020). While that study found 93 genes that were required for survival in one or more strains, remarkably only three genes were common to all four strains: rfaH, lpp, and arnD.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: arnD was not required for serum resistance in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Comparison with our dataset revealed that in contrast to rfaH, arnD was not required for serum resistance in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the experimental data with published literature.

claim: Comparison of the K. pneumoniae ECL8 serum resistome data with the multidrug-resistant E. coli strain EC958 revealed 14 genes in common.
source: Surprisingly, comparison of our data with the 56 genes comprising the serum resistome of the more distantly related multidrug-resistant E. coli strain EC958 revealed 14 genes in common.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the experimental data with published literature.

claim: Mutation of five genes (ompA, galE, exbB, exbD, and sodA) conferred reduced fitness for both growth in urine and survival in serum in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Despite the intra- and interspecies variation in the serum resistome noted above, comparison of the urinome and serum resistome of K. pneumoniae ECL8 revealed that mutation of five genes (ompA, galE, exbB, exbD, and sodA) conferred reduced fitness for both growth in urine and survival in serum.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the urine and serum TraDIS data.

claim: A role for OmpA in serum resistance has previously been described for E. coli.
source: Notably, a role for OmpA in serum resistance has previously been described for E. coli, however it was not identified by TraDIS experiments investigating the serum resistome (Phan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: GalE is known to play a key role in serum resistance for E. coli and Salmonella spp.
source: GalE is known to play a key role in serum resistance for E. coli and Salmonella spp.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: GalE plays a role in D-galactan II synthesis, an O1 LPS component in K. pneumoniae.
source: It has been previously reported that GalE plays a role in D-galactan II synthesis, an O1 LPS component in K. pneumoniae (Ramos et al., 2012; Clarke and Whitfield, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Loss of galE results in a modified LPS in K. pneumoniae resulting in increased serum susceptibility.
source: These data suggest that loss of galE results in a modified LPS in K. pneumoniae resulting in increased serum susceptibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and known function of galE.

claim: The manganese-dependent superoxide dismutase SodA converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen to prevent DNA and other cellular damage.
source: Additionally, the manganese-dependent superoxide dismutase SodA converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide and oxygen to prevent DNA and other cellular damage (Touati, 1983; Doukyu and Taguchi, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: sodA is expressed in response to anaerobic challenge and high-oxygen concentration in K. pneumoniae.
source: A previous study in K. pneumoniae has reported the inducible expression of sodA in a triumvirate system with sodB and sodC, expressed in response to anaerobic challenge and high-oxygen concentration (Najmuldeen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The observed importance of sodA might be a consequence of elevated levels of reactive oxygen species due to iron acquisition.
source: Hence, the observed importance of sodA might be a consequence of elevated levels of reactive oxygen species due to iron acquisition and could represent a specialized metabolic adaptation for growth in these environments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: These findings underline the interplay between bacterial iron homeostasis and oxidative stress previously reported in Gram-negative bacteria.
source: Ultimately, these findings underline the interplay between bacterial iron homeostasis and oxidative stress previously reported in Gram-negative bacteria (Cornelis et al., 2011; Adler et al., 2014; Peralta et al., 2016; Guest et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cross-niche genes (i.e. urine and serum) and associated pathways are suitable drug development targets to treat Klebsiella infections.
source: However, these data shine a light on cross-niche (i.e. urine and serum) genes and associated pathways as suitable drug development targets to treat Klebsiella infections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Transposon insertion orientation bias into gnd lends further credence to a transcriptional regulatory model where biosynthesis of O-antigen and capsule is coupled for biophysical reasons.
source: As the downstream transcriptional unit of gnd are O-antigen-related genes (i.e. biosynthesis and export), this in turn lends further credence to a transcriptional regulatory model where biosynthesis of O-antigen and capsule is coupled for biophysical reasons as has been previously reported (Dorman et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and supported by citations.

claim: O-antigen biosynthesis genes (i.e. wabI and waaL) play a contributing role in serum resistance in K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Collectively, these data show that O-antigen biosynthesis genes (i.e. wabI and waaL) play a contributing role in serum resistance while hns mutants were shown to be more resistant to serum killing than WT K. pneumoniae ECL8.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: hns mutants were shown to be more resistant to serum killing than wild-type K. pneumoniae ECL8.
source: Collectively, these data show that O-antigen biosynthesis genes (i.e. wabI and waaL) play a contributing role in serum resistance while hns mutants were shown to be more resistant to serum killing than WT K. pneumoniae ECL8.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: This is the first report of a role for hns in resisting complement-mediated killing in human serum.
source: Despite the previously described links between hns and the regulation of a selection of capsular genes (Dorman et al., 2018; Ares et al., 2016), this is the first report of a role for hns in resisting complement-mediated killing in human serum.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding, supported by citations to previous work.
